chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Chapter 26 asks what a family does after it better understands a child's internal triggers. Eyal's answer is to make time for traction together. In the book's language, traction means actions aligned with values and prior intent, and that logic can guide family life as well as adult work.

That is why the chapter resists generic family calendar advice. The point is not simply that parents should schedule everything. The stronger move is visible, shared routines and agreements that children can understand, help shape, or at least meaningfully anticipate. The family starts deciding before the moment of distraction.

The chapter matters because shared traction reduces conflict later. Homework, play, rest, chores, family connection, and personal time become less likely to be negotiated only in the heat of temptation. The family has something clearer to return to when the pull of distraction shows up.

The chapter also keeps values central. The goal is not maximum efficiency or total household control. A family plan should reflect what matters to the people in it. Without that link, the chapter turns into command-and-control scheduling.

That is why the shared-contract logic matters. Children do not need equal power over every decision, but traction together works better when routines feel legible, visible, and connected to real priorities rather than arbitrary enforcement.

That prepares Chapter 27 naturally. Once shared traction is clearer, the family can begin shaping external triggers around those commitments instead of only reacting after distraction arrives.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Chapter 26 argues that traction can be built together in family life through shared planning tied to values and prior intent. The chapter moves from understanding children's inner triggers to making visible routines that reduce conflict when distraction appears.

This matters because families often negotiate values only at the moment of temptation. Shared routines and legible expectations create a better starting point than reactive enforcement.

The chapter also avoids command language. It is not generic scheduling advice. The plan should be collaborative enough that children can understand it and see why it exists.

The chapter keeps values above efficiency. Family traction should protect what matters, not simply create a more controllable household.

That is why the next chapter can move into external triggers. Shared traction gives the family something concrete to protect environmentally.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Chapter 26 stops asking the family to improvise every important decision at the exact second distraction shows up. Eyal's answer is traction together: a visible route, built in advance, tied to what the family actually cares about.

That is why the chapter refuses to become generic family-calendar bureaucracy. A command post is not the point. The point is shared routine, legible commitment, and enough collaboration that the child can see the map instead of only the enforcement.

This matters because reactive families keep arguing about values in the heat of temptation. Shared traction lets the family decide earlier, when everybody is less hijacked.

The chapter also keeps its moral center. This is not about squeezing maximum efficiency out of a household. It is about protecting what matters together.

That is why external triggers come next. Once the route is visible, the family can start moving furniture so the hallway stops ambushing the plan.
